summary: Records Pip's header processing, as a companion to the near-term architecture described in RFC 1621. The aim is to preserve the ideas of Pip, good and bad. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: The second half of notes about an unused design for the Internet, describing how its address labels are read.

questions: what is the pip transit part
subtitle: The Pip packet header and how hosts and routers process it, recorded after the Pip project ended.

tldr.problem: A general-purpose internet protocol needed a header that could carry many kinds of routing, addressing and handling without being redesigned for each one.
tldr.mechanism: Pip splits its header into an Initial Part, one or more Transit Parts and an Options Part. Routers walk a chain of 16-bit forwarding indexes through tables to find a Forwarding Information Block.
tldr.outcome: Pip was merged into SIPP and this RFC only preserves its ideas. It is Historic, and any text presenting Pip as the replacement for IP should be ignored.

today: RFC 1622 is Historic. It was published after the Pip project ended and Pip was merged with SIP to form SIPP, and it exists to record Pip's ideas. The architecture around this header is in RFC 1621.

sections.title: Pip as a Machine Language for Networks
sections.content:
This RFC defines Pip header processing for routers and hosts. Its preamble explains that Pip was one of the candidate replacements for IP in 1992 and 1993, was merged with SIP to create SIPP in mid 1993, and that the text is kept to record the ideas of Pip, good and bad. The remainder is taken from the last Pip draft, so any text calling Pip the intended replacement for IP should be ignored.

The author's central idea is that Pip strips as much functional semantics as possible out of the base specification. Pip defines a header and forwarding rules that can support many routing, addressing and flow styles, the way a machine language defines actions without saying what a program is for. Questions such as how to do a particular thing with Pip belong in companion documents like RFC 1621. The conventions section states that all functions in the specification are mandatory.
sections.plainLanguage: Pip is like the plain set of building blocks in a toy set. It does not say what to build. Other papers explain the buildings.

sections.title: The Three-Part Header and the Initial Part
sections.content:
A Pip header has an Initial Part, a Transit Part and an Options Part, each starting on a 32-bit boundary, with the Transit Part on a 64-bit boundary. Tunneling is built in: a Transit Part is encapsulated in another Transit Part, so a tunneled packet has one Transit Part for each nested tunnel.

The Initial Part has a 4-bit Version set to 8, a 4-bit Sub-Version, and 8-bit Options Offset, Options Contents and Options Present fields. It continues with a 16-bit Packet SubID, a 16-bit Protocol, a 64-bit Dest ID, a 64-bit Source ID, a 32-bit Payload Length, an 8-bit Host Version, an 8-bit Payload Offset and a 16-bit Hop Count. The Protocol values are those used for IPv4.

The Version of 8 was an experimental number assigned for Pip development, so IP encapsulation schemes can work for Pip. A packet with an unknown Version is silently discarded. A router also discards a Version 8 packet with an unknown Sub-Version. A host that sees an unknown Sub-Version processes only the Initial Part and Options Part and does not parse the Transit Part.

A router decrements the Hop Count. If a system that is not the recipient sees a Hop Count of 0, it discards the packet and routes a PCMP Destination Unreachable message back. The Packet SubID lets a host match PCMP messages to the right flow, since the Transit Part can change in transit. The Dest ID is compared in full with the system's own IDs, and a mismatch triggers an ID/RD Mismatch PCMP message to flush the ID to routing binding in the source.
sections.plainLanguage: The first part of the label says what kind of packet it is, who sent it, who it is for, how big it is, and how many more hops it may take before being thrown away.

sections.title: The Transit Part and Forwarding
sections.content:
The Transit Part has a Transit Part Offset, an HD Contents field, the 32-bit Handling Directive (HD), and the Routing Directive (RD). The RD consists of an FTIF Offset, an RC Contents field, a 16-bit Routing Context (RC) and a chain of 16-bit Forwarding Table Index Fields (FTIFs), padded to a 32-bit boundary. The HD triggers handling, such as low priority queueing, and never influences the next hop. The RD only decides how to forward and never influences handling. Systems may modify the HD, which the RFC calls packet tagging.

The mapping from a Contents value to the layout of the HD or RC is stored locally. Any of 256 Contents values can be active at a given time. For an HD unit that a system does not understand, it knows whether to pass it on untouched, set it to all 0s, set it to all 1s, discard the packet silently, or discard it with a PCMP HDU Not Understood message.

The router algorithm starts with the RC, which indexes an rcTable chosen by the RC Contents. The instruction found there can be to decapsulate, to forward with a given Forwarding Information Block (FIB), to look at the Dest ID, or to examine the FTIF chain. In the chain, each FTIF indexes a forwarding table and gives the same options, plus moving on to the next FTIF. Finally the router prunes the set of potential recipients listed in the FIB and builds a new header for each remaining next hop by modifying the RC, the current FTIF, the FTIF Offset and any encapsulations.
sections.plainLanguage: The middle part of the label is a set of directions. A router looks up the first direction in a table, which may point it to another table, until it finds which road to take.

sections.title: The Options Part
sections.content:
Options are found through the Initial Part. Options Present has one bit for each of up to eight options, and the local mapping named by Options Contents says which option each bit means. For example, a value of 101 could mean that two options are present and one is absent. A value of 0 means no options, whatever the Options Contents value is. At the time of writing, the RFC says only one option existed.

The Options Part begins with a 64-bit Options Descriptor, made of eight 8-bit Option Position fields that give each option's offset in 32-bit words. Every option is at least one 32-bit word long and ends on a 32-bit word boundary. Option types are not marked in the options themselves, and there is no common format, because each option has its own format defined in another specification.

This design means a router can ignore options that do not affect it, such as a PDN address option on a router not attached to a PDN, and can jump straight to a wanted option instead of scanning a list.
sections.plainLanguage: The extras section has a little table of contents at the front, so a router only reads the extras that matter to it and skips the rest.

fields.name: Sub-Version
fields.desc: Refers only to the Transit Part; 0 in this specification.

fields.name: Options Offset
fields.desc: Position of the Options Part, in 32-bit words.

fields.name: Options Contents
fields.desc: Says how Options Present is interpreted.

fields.name: Options Present
fields.desc: Which of up to eight options are present.

fields.name: Packet SubID
fields.desc: Lets hosts match PCMP messages to a flow.

fields.name: Protocol
fields.desc: Protocol in the payload, using IPv4 values.

fields.name: Dest ID
fields.desc: Pip ID of the final recipient.

fields.name: Payload Length
fields.desc: Payload length in 8-bit units, excluding the header.

fields.name: Host Version
fields.desc: Which Pip software features the sending host has.

fields.name: Payload Offset
fields.desc: Position of the payload, in 32-bit words.

layers.detail: Handling Directive and Routing Directive; one per nested tunnel
